text: DeepStateMap is a Ukrainian war map run by the DeepState UA NGO and fed largely by Ukrainian military sources.
DeepStateMap is deliberately published 2–3 days late for operational security.

observations.subject: DeepStateMap

text: DeepStateMap's visual grammar is simple: semi-transparent area fills show control status (occupied, liberated, recently liberated, unknown/grey, pre-2022 occupied).
On DeepStateMap, point icons mark Russian units, airfields and HQs, and arrows show "directions of attack".
DeepStateMap never shows Ukrainian positions.
The ISW/CTP map is the Western reference map of the war; its legend is epistemic rather than just territorial, separating assessed (evidence-backed) from claimed (asserted, unverified) areas.

text: Since December 2025 the ISW/CTP map draws a dedicated infiltration-areas layer.

text: Most Western outlets, for example the BBC, redraw ISW/CTP data rather than map the front themselves.

From 2025 on, drone kill zones and infiltration by small Russian groups turned the grey zone from a thin no-man's-land into a deep contact zone with overlapping positions: the front line stopped being a line.
The deepening grey zone forced DeepState (2026) and ISW (December 2025) to redefine their map uncertainty categories.

text: DeepState has clashed publicly with Ukrainian commanders over encirclements and breakthroughs, at Makarivka (December 2024) and Dobropillia (August 2025).
Flag-planting photo-ops by both sides are an information-war tactic that careful mappers refuse to map.
Delta is the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence's situational-awareness system, one of the Ukrainian military's own digital layers.
Kropyva is an Army SOS artillery and mapping tablet app used by the Ukrainian military.
Vezha is a drone-stream module of the Ukrainian military's digital systems, running the Avengers AI.
The Army of Drones Bonus "e-points" system turned video-verified strikes into a points economy with unit leaderboards and a marketplace.
DeepState's undocumented history endpoint serves the full GeoJSON of every DeepStateMap version since 3 April 2022.

Differencing DeepStateMap month-end versions reproduces DeepState's own published monthly territory figures to within a few km² in most months, and gives Russian gains and Ukrainian recaptures separately.
DeepState has no documented API or open licence, although undocumented JSON endpoints exist and community scrapers use them.

DeepState UA (ДіпСтейт), the operator of DeepStateMap, is a Ukrainian NGO co-founded by childhood friends Roman Pohorilyi (law background) and Ruslan Mykula (marketing).
DeepState began in February 2020 as a Telegram channel on world news and politics.
The DeepState team experimented with an updatable conflict map during the 2021 Taliban offensive.
Before the full-scale invasion, DeepState switched to tracking Russian forces on Ukraine's borders.
DeepStateMap went live on 24 February 2022, the first day of the full-scale invasion.
DeepStateMap first ran on Google Maps; Google blocked the account in late March 2022, so DeepState built its own platform and map data from before 3 April 2022 was lost.
DeepStateMap's own version history starts on 3 April 2022, consistent with the loss of earlier data after the Google block.
DeepState has 100+ paid staff and volunteers working from an undisclosed location in Kyiv.

text: In the computed series, all areas are clipped to Ukraine's land (the geoBoundaries border intersected with Natural Earth 10 m land) and measured in a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on Ukraine.
In the computed series, Russian gain is area newly red since the previous month-end, Ukrainian recapture is area red at the previous month-end but not now, and net is the change in total red area.
A 150 m morphological opening removes redraw slivers from the computed gains and recaptures; it changes monthly totals by under 5%.

NATO APP-6 (STANAG 2019) and US MIL-STD-2525 are aligned military symbology standards; APP-6A (1999) is equivalent to MIL-STD-2525A.
Later APP-6 editions are APP-6B (2008) and APP-6C (2011), and APP-6E is listed as current.
milsymbol supports MIL-STD-2525C/D/E, FM 1-02.2 and APP-6 B/D/E.
In APP-6 and MIL-STD-2525, affiliation is encoded twice, by frame shape and by colour.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a friend unit is drawn with a rectangle frame in blue.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a hostile unit is drawn with a diamond frame in red.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a neutral unit is drawn with a square frame in green.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a unknown unit is drawn with a quatrefoil frame in yellow.
APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 have further affiliation states: pending, assumed friend, suspect, and exercise variants.
Because the frame shape carries affiliation as well as colour, APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbols work in monochrome.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525, a solid frame means present and a dashed frame means planned/anticipated.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525, closed frames denote land and sea surface, bottom-open frames air/space, and top-open frames subsurface.

An APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbol consists of a frame, a central icon and an optional fill, with modifiers/amplifiers arranged around the frame: unique designation, additional information, altitude/depth, combat effectiveness, headquarters/task force/dummy, and echelon/mobility.

Echelons are coded in the SIDC and drawn above the frame: Team/Crew, Squad, Section, Platoon/detachment, Company/battery/troop, Battalion/squadron, Regiment/group, Brigade, Division, Corps, Army, Army Group/front, Region/Theatre, Command.
Older symbology standards use letter-based symbol identification codes (SIDCs), 15 characters long in the APP-6A lineage.
